summaries.example: Imagine your class can spend its last $20 on either decorations for a party or meals for several hungry students. A consequentialist would ask which choice leads to the best overall results. The answer may depend on how much good and harm each choice creates, not simply on what the money was originally meant for.
summaries.summary: Consequentialism is the idea that what is morally right depends on consequences, or results. The most famous version is classic utilitarianism. It says an action is right when it produces more total good than any other available action. Early utilitarians often described good as pleasure and bad as pain. Later thinkers proposed other values, such as knowledge, friendship, freedom, fairness, rights, and abilities. They also disagreed about whose results count, whether to add everyone’s benefits together, and whether to judge an action by its actual or expected results. Some versions focus on rules or motives because a rule allowing harmful actions could create bad results when many people follow it. Critics worry that consequentialism might permit unfair treatment, ignore rights, or demand that people always sacrifice their own plans. Supporters reply that consequences can explain why many moral rules are useful and why helping make the world better matters. The entry presents these arguments without claiming that one version settles every disagreement.
key_ideas: Consequentialism says that the results of an action are central to deciding whether it is right.
Classic utilitarianism says we should choose the action with the greatest total good for everyone, often understood as more pleasure and less pain.
Not every consequentialist thinks pleasure is the only good. Some also value knowledge, friendship, freedom, fairness, or life.
Philosophers disagree about whether we should look at actual results, likely results, or what people could reasonably expect.
Some versions use rules, motives, or character instead of looking only at the action by itself.
A major question is whether consequentialism asks people to give up too much of their time, money, or personal choices.
summaries.why_it_matters: Consequentialism gives us a clear way to ask, “What will this choice do?” It can help people think about effects on everyone, not just themselves. It also shows why moral decisions can be difficult: a choice may help some people while hurting others, and good results can be hard to predict. Studying the theory helps us compare ideas about fairness, kindness, rules, rights, and personal freedom.

important_terms.definition: A view about what is right or wrong that looks mainly at what happens because of an action.
The idea that pleasure is the only basic good and pain is the only basic bad.
The total good left after the bad results are taken away.
A result that is allowed but is not required. It is considered especially helpful or generous.

questions_to_think_about: Should the choice with the best results always be the right choice?
Can something be valuable even if it does not make anyone feel happier?
Is it fair to count everyone’s good equally?
How much should we help strangers when we also have our own needs?
Would a good rule sometimes be better than making a new calculation each time?

summaries.example: A hospital has five patients who each need a different organ, while another healthy patient could be killed so that the organs could be used. In a simplified version of the case, performing the transplant would save five lives and end one life. A direct, maximizing consequentialist might judge the action by comparing the total outcomes and could reach a disturbing conclusion. Critics argue that the healthy patient’s rights matter independently of the total outcome. Rule consequentialists might ask whether publicly accepting a rule permitting such operations would damage trust in doctors and hospitals. The case shows why consequentialists debate values, rights, agency, and rules.
summaries.summary: Consequentialism holds that normative properties depend only on consequences. In moral theory, this usually means that an act’s rightness depends on the results of the act or on consequences connected with it. Classic utilitarianism is the paradigm: it combines act consequentialism with maximization, total aggregation, universal and equal consideration, agent-neutrality, and hedonism. The entry stresses that these commitments are logically separable. A consequentialist may replace hedonism with preference satisfaction or a pluralistic account including knowledge, friendship, freedom, justice, rights, or capabilities. The theory may compare total value, average value, distributions, or whole outcomes rather than simply adding every benefit and harm. It may also assess actual, expected, intended, foreseeable, or probable consequences. This matters because an agent can reasonably choose a helpful act that later produces an unforeseeable disaster. Consequentialism faces objections concerning organ-transplant cases, promises, friendship, rights, fairness, and the demandingness of morality. Responses include agent-relative value, rule consequentialism, satisficing, progressive, and scalar versions. Supporters appeal to the thought that we should make the world better, to explanatory success concerning moral intuitions, and to arguments from equality, rationality, universalizability, or impartial choice. The entry concludes that these arguments leave consequentialism a serious live option, not a conclusively established theory.
key_ideas: Consequentialism is a family of theories, not one completely uniform doctrine. Theories may disagree about value, aggregation, persons, rules, and the agent’s perspective while still focusing on consequences.
Classic utilitarianism combines several commitments: act evaluation, maximizing, total aggregation, equal consideration, universal scope, agent-neutrality, and a hedonistic account of value.
Consequentialists debate whether value consists in pleasure, preference satisfaction, welfare, capabilities, rights, justice, virtue, knowledge, or several of these together.
A criterion of rightness need not be a decision procedure. A theory may say what makes an act right without requiring people to calculate every consequence before acting.
Actual, intended, foreseen, foreseeable, and probable consequences can produce different moral judgments, especially when an unforeseeable accident occurs.
Rights and fairness create pressure for indirect or agent-relative forms of consequentialism, including rule consequentialism, but these modifications generate their own difficulties.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory forces careful attention to who is affected by a decision, how harms and benefits should be compared, and how uncertainty should influence judgment. It also exposes tensions that appear in public policy and ordinary life: impartiality versus special obligations, aggregate welfare versus distribution, and moral ideals versus personal liberty. Even if one rejects consequentialism, its arguments can clarify why outcomes matter and why moral rules need justification. The disagreements also show that changing one part of a moral theory can produce a substantially different theory.

important_terms.definition: The claim that a moral property, such as rightness, depends only on consequences.
The view that an action is right exactly when it produces at least as much good as any available alternative.
The view that pleasure is intrinsically good and pain intrinsically bad.
A theory that treats several things—such as knowledge, friendship, freedom, or fairness—as basic values.
A theory that evaluates an act by its actual results rather than by what was expected or reasonably foreseeable.
A theory in which the rightness of an act depends on consequences associated with a rule, motive, or virtue rather than only that act itself.
The claim that an act can be assessed differently from the perspective of the agent who performs it and from that of an observer.
The objection that maximizing good may require too many sacrifices of personal projects, relationships, time, or resources.

questions_to_think_about: If saving five people requires intentionally killing one innocent person, should the numerical difference decide the case? Why or why not?
Can a theory remain consequentialist if it gives rights or rules priority over happiness in some situations?
Is it coherent to say that an action is objectively wrong even when the agent could not reasonably have predicted its bad result?
Would a rule that generally protects trust produce better consequences than a rule allowing rare exceptions with excellent expected results?
Does the fact that a theory explains some moral judgments give us a reason to accept it, or only a reason to keep considering it?

summaries.example: Suppose your school has money for one project. It can buy better sports equipment for a small team or provide quiet study spaces that many students can use. A consequentialist would compare the results: how much benefit each choice creates, for whom, and how serious any disadvantages are. One version might add up the total benefits. Another might give extra weight to students who are struggling most. A rule-based version might ask which general school rule about spending money would work best if schools followed it often.
summaries.summary: Consequentialism is a family of moral views built around one central idea: consequences determine moral rightness. Classic utilitarianism is its best-known form. It says that an action is right when it produces the greatest total balance of good over bad for all affected people. Traditional utilitarians often identify good with pleasure and bad with pain, but later consequentialists have proposed preference satisfaction, knowledge, friendship, freedom, fairness, rights, capabilities, and other values. They also disagree about whether to add all benefits together, focus on average well-being, consider how goods are distributed, or compare whole outcomes. Another disagreement concerns evidence. A theory might look at what actually happens, what was likely to happen, or what the agent intended or could reasonably foresee. The entry distinguishes a standard for judging rightness from a decision method. Consequentialism need not tell people to perform a giant calculation before every choice; familiar rules or moral habits might usually lead to better results. Critics argue that maximizing can permit actions that violate rights, break promises, neglect friends, or demand constant sacrifice. Consequentialists respond with views that emphasize rules, motives, virtues, the agent’s perspective, or doing enough good rather than the absolute maximum. These responses are themselves debated. Arguments for consequentialism include the importance of improving the world, explaining moral judgments, and reasoning from impartiality and equality. None is presented as a final proof.
key_ideas: Consequentialism focuses on results, but versions differ about which results count as good and how they should be compared.
Classic utilitarianism treats pleasure and pain as the basic values and adds up the effects on all people.
Some consequentialists value preferences, knowledge, freedom, relationships, fairness, rights, or other goods instead of—or as well as—pleasure.
The theory may use actual results or expected results. Supporters often say the rule is a standard for judging actions, not a demand to calculate everything in advance.
Critics use cases involving innocent people, promises, friendship, and charity to argue that consequences alone may overlook rights or personal commitments.
Rule, agent-relative, satisficing, and other forms try to answer these criticisms, but philosophers disagree about whether the changes solve the problems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Consequentialism gives students a practical lens for examining difficult decisions. It asks them to look beyond intentions and consider real effects on different people, including people who are easy to overlook. At the same time, its challenges help explain why ethical thinking also discusses rights, trust, fairness, relationships, and reasonable limits on sacrifice. Learning the theory is useful not only for deciding whether it is correct, but also for understanding the structure of disagreements about what morality should require.

important_terms.definition: The view that what is morally right depends only on consequences, or what follows from an action or related choice.
A famous form of consequentialism that says we should choose the action producing the greatest total good for everyone.
The idea that pleasure is valuable in itself and pain is bad in itself.
The idea that several kinds of things may be valuable, such as knowledge, friendship, freedom, fairness, or life.
A moral theory that judges an action by the consequences of that action itself.
A moral theory that asks what would happen if people generally accepted or followed a rule.
The view that similar benefits should count similarly, no matter who receives them.
The concern that a moral theory may require people to give up nearly all ordinary personal choices in order to do the most good.

questions_to_think_about: Should the same benefit count equally if it goes to a friend and to a stranger?
Is a bad result enough to make an action wrong when the person acted carefully and could not predict it?
Could following a useful rule sometimes lead to worse results in one unusual case?
Are there limits to how much people should be expected to give up for others?
Which seems more important in a hard choice: the total amount of good, how it is shared, or whether anyone’s rights are broken?
